DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — PYRIDOSTIGMINE WITH METHOTREXATE AND HYDROXYCHLOROQUINE

Query: Adding pyridostigmine to regimen including methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine

FINDINGS:
  PYRIDOSTIGMINE + METHOTREXATE: No clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction identified.

results.content:
LITERATURE SEARCH: Brown Syndrome vs Ocular Neuromuscular Junction Disease — Diagnostic Pitfalls

KEY FINDINGS:
1. BROWN SYNDROME: Restriction of superior oblique tendon sheath causing limited elevation in adduction; typically unilateral; MRI shows no EOM enlargement or tendon inflammation in idiopathic cases; may be idiopathic, inflammatory, or traumatic.
2. OCULAR NMJ DISEASE: Can present with vertical strabismus and restricted elevation that mimics Brown syndrome; distinguishing features include ice pack test response, fatigability, diurnal variation, and Cogan lid twitch.
3. BILATERAL BROWN SYNDROME IN ADULTS: Rare; bilateral adult-onset presentation without a clear mechanical cause has been reported in the context of NMJ disease.
4. CASE REPORTS: Multiple reports exist of NMJ disease initially characterised as Brown syndrome prior to NMJ evaluation; progression to ptosis and bulbar symptoms is a reported clinical trajectory.
5. MANAGEMENT SHIFT: Diagnosis of NMJ disease leads to different pharmacological management than connective tissue-related motility disorders.
results.title: Clinical literature

output.summary: Bilateral adult-onset Brown syndrome without structural correlate should trigger NMJ evaluation; ice pack test and AChR antibody testing are key diagnostic steps.

results.content:
LITERATURE SEARCH: MGTX Trial — Thymectomy in Non-Thymomatous Generalized MG

MGTX TRIAL (Wolfe GI et al., NEJM 2016):
  Population: AChR-positive generalized MG patients aged 18–65 without thymoma
  Results: Thymectomy + prednisone vs prednisone alone
  Primary outcome: Thymectomy group had significantly lower quantitative MG score over 3 years
  Secondary outcome: Less prednisone required; fewer treatment failures; fewer hospitalizations
  ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Age 18–65, AChR-positive, generalized MG, no thymoma on imaging

output.summary: MGTX trial (NEJM 2016) demonstrated benefit of thymectomy plus prednisone over prednisone alone in AChR-positive generalized MG patients aged 18–65 without thymoma.

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG
Do NOT administer IV magnesium for MG patients (e.g., for hypomagnesaemia, eclampsia prophylaxis) without alternative — blocks NMJ transmission
Do NOT use non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without hospitalization or pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable weakness to a functional disorder before completing serology + RNS + single-fiber EMG workup
required_recommendations: Confirm AChR antibody positivity — overturns Brown syndrome label
RNS and SFEMG to confirm NMJ pathology

avoided_actions.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

accepted: AChR antibody-positive generalized myasthenia gravis, initially misdiagnosed as acquired Brown syndrome

differential.diagnosis: True acquired Brown syndrome (superior oblique tendon disorder)
differential.key_features: MRI here without orbital pathology; fatigable diurnal pattern not explained by mechanical tendon restriction.
Hypothyroidism on levothyroxine; no proptosis; pattern is fatigable.
No baseline CMAP reduction; AChR positive.

key_clinical_evidence: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
Atypical strabismus patterns that fluctuate should always raise MG suspicion — vertical diplopia in MG is recognized but under-diagnosed.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 47-year-old woman with hypothyroidism and polycystic ovarian syndrome presented for re-evaluation of persistent and worsening binocular diplopia and restriction of eye elevation. Eight weeks prior to the current admission, she had noticed binocular vertical diplopia that was worst when looking to the right. Ophthalmology initially identified a left hypotropia of 4 prism diopters and mild limitation of elevation of the left eye in adduction, and made a diagnosis of acquired Brown syndrome (restriction of the superior oblique tendon sheath). She was started on ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily and later prednisolone 25 mg daily; she had some pain relief but persistent motility deficit.

Over the following month, the motility deficit progressed to bilateral moderate limitation of elevation in adduction. Two repeat MRI studies of the brain and orbits showed no superior oblique hypertrophy, tendon inflammation, or trochlear attachment abnormality. Serological testing for SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, and mixed connective tissue disease was negative. She continued on oral prednisolone up to 50 mg daily and later methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine without significant improvement.

Now, 8 months after the initial presentation, she has also developed bilateral upper eyelid ptosis (noticed by her husband over the past 3 weeks), increasing difficulty finishing a meal due to jaw fatigue, and a muffled nasal voice quality that worsens with prolonged speaking. She recalls that the ptosis seems more pronounced in the late afternoon. She has had no prior ophthalmic surgery or trauma. On examination, bilateral ptosis was now evident (right greater than left), along with bilateral restriction of elevation in adduction. The ice pack test applied for 5 minutes produced a 4 mm improvement in ptosis bilaterally. The SLURP test was positive for fatigable palate elevation.
